meta.title: Who really said "Seventy-two suburbs in search of a city"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: The famous put-down of Los Angeles is pinned on Dorothy Parker. Wikiquote files it under Misattributed, and no documented first use has been found.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Seventy-two suburbs in search of a city'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Dorothy Parker, on the available evidence. Wikiquote lists it as misattributed; the earliest documented use is still unknown.

answer.label: Not Dorothy Parker — origin unknown
answer.authorDates: Unattributed quip about Los Angeles · no documented first use located
answer.sourceLine: The line travels as Dorothy Parker’s verdict on Los Angeles, but nothing pins it to her. Wikiquote files it under Misattributed ↗ and suggests it derives from a phrase of Aldous Huxley’s. We could not confirm that antecedent, and we found no documented first use of this wording by anyone — so no author is claimed here.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: 72 suburbs in search of a city
trail: Wikiquote’s Dorothy Parker page ↗ lists “72 suburbs in search of a city” in its Misattributed section. That section opens with an editors’ warning that “a great many misquotations are attributed to Dorothy Parker” and asks readers to verify provenance before ascribing anything to her.

Wikiquote suggests the description is “based on” Aldous Huxley calling Los Angeles “nineteen suburbs in search of a metropolis” in a 1925 book it names as Americana, adding that Huxley “was likely quoting someone else”. We could not confirm that citation: no Huxley book called Americana could be located, and his Wikiquote page ↗ records his travel book of the period as Jesting Pilate: The Diary of a Journey (1926). We report Wikiquote’s suggestion as Wikiquote’s, not as established fact.

We looked inside the Huxley book to settle it and could not. The Internet Archive’s scan of Jesting Pilate ↗ (London: Chatto & Windus) is lending-restricted, so its contents cannot be searched from here. An Internet Archive item search for “suburbs in search of a metropolis” also returned no match — but that index does not reach inside scanned books, so it settles nothing about what the book actually contains.

Quote Investigator, which has investigated several other quips pinned on Parker, has no article on this phrase — a site search returned no matches. So the strongest available finding remains Wikiquote’s: widely credited to Parker, not hers, origin open. Wikipedia’s biography of Parker ↗ does not mention the line either.
source.excerptNote: That is the wording as it stands in Wikiquote’s Misattributed section ↗. The spelled-out “Seventy-two” form is the one that circulates most widely online; neither has been traced to a dated first printing.
source.rightsNote: No copyright status is asserted, because the wording has not been tied to any identified publication or author. If a first printing is ever located, its date would decide the question; until then we claim nothing. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Dorothy Parker
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Dorothy Parker
author.metaLine: 1893–1967 · American poet, critic and short-story writer
author.bio: Dorothy Parker (born Dorothy Rothschild, 22 August 1893 — 7 June 1967) was an American poet, critic and short-story writer, and a founding member of the Algonquin Round Table. Her reputation for the devastating one-liner is exactly why orphaned wisecracks drift to her: a sharp, city-sized insult sounds like Parker, and that resemblance is doing all the work here. Wikiquote’s editors thought the problem serious enough to head her Misattributed section with a standing warning about it.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: It is one of the most quoted insults ever aimed at Los Angeles, and it almost always arrives with Dorothy Parker’s name on it. That credit has no source behind it.

items.why: Wikiquote lists the line under Misattributed ↗ on her page, whose editors also warn that a great many misquotations are ascribed to her and ask that provenance be checked first.

Wikiquote suggests the line is based on Huxley calling Los Angeles “nineteen suburbs in search of a metropolis”, citing a 1925 book Americana. We could not confirm that a Huxley book of that title and year exists; his period travel book ↗ is Jesting Pilate (1926). Wikiquote itself adds that Huxley “was likely quoting someone else”.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer is that nobody knows who said it first. Parker is the name it carries, not the name behind it — see Wikiquote’s entry ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The joke works by borrowing a shape everyone already knew: Pirandello’s Six Characters in Search of an Author had made “N somethings in search of a something” a ready-made template for describing anything that felt incomplete. Applied to Los Angeles it captured a real complaint of the 1920s and 1930s — that the city had arrived at metropolitan scale without ever growing a centre.

Because the template is so easy to refill, the number kept moving. Wikiquote records a nineteen-suburb version; the form that survived is seventy-two. A line that mutates freely is a line with no fixed author, which is roughly what the evidence shows here.
detailsBody: We have deliberately left this page thinner than the claim usually is elsewhere. The common retelling names a specific Huxley book and year; we could not verify that book, so we do not repeat it as fact. Naming a source we have not seen would be the exact failure this site exists to correct — and a confident citation is precisely how an unsourced quip acquires a respectable-looking pedigree in the first place.
context.pull: A line that mutates freely is a line with no fixed author.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote lists "72 suburbs in search of a city" in the Misattributed section of its Dorothy Parker page, and proposes an Aldous Huxley antecedent while noting he was likely quoting someone else.
Wikiquote's Aldous Huxley page records his travel book of the period as Jesting Pilate: The Diary of a Journey (1926); it contains no 'suburbs in search of a metropolis' line.
The Internet Archive holds a scan of Huxley's Jesting Pilate; the Diary of a Journey, published London: Chatto & Windus. The item is lending-restricted and not full-text searchable.
Wikipedia gives Dorothy Parker as born Dorothy Rothschild, 22 August 1893, died 7 June 1967, an American poet, critic and screenwriter and a founding member of the Algonquin Round Table.
Wikipedia gives Aldous Leonard Huxley, 26 July 1894 – 22 November 1963, an English writer and philosopher.
